title: Water Transport and Transpiration Core Test
description: Connect roots, xylem, and leaves to water movement and evaluate evidence about plant water loss.

questions.prompt: A plant takes up water through its roots. Which route best models its movement to leaves?
questions.questionText: A plant takes up water through its roots. Which route best models its movement to leaves?
options: Soil -> leaves -> roots -> air.
Soil -> roots -> xylem -> leaves.
Air -> sugar -> roots -> xylem.
Roots -> sunlight -> leaves.
questions.correctAnswer: Soil -> roots -> xylem -> leaves.
questions.explanation: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals through the plant.

questions.prompt: What is transpiration?
questions.questionText: What is transpiration?
options: Absorption of every mineral by roots.
Production of sugar from light alone.
Loss of water vapor from plant surfaces, mainly leaves.
Loss of liquid rainwater from a leaf's surface.
questions.correctAnswer: Loss of water vapor from plant surfaces, mainly leaves.
questions.explanation: Transpiration involves water leaving the plant as vapor; rain evaporating from its exterior is a different source.

questions.prompt: Why can leaves lose water even when no droplets are visible?
questions.questionText: Why can leaves lose water even when no droplets are visible?
options: Water vapor is an invisible gas.
All water loss must occur as visible drops.
Water turns directly into sunlight.
Leaves cannot lose water without tearing.
questions.correctAnswer: Water vapor is an invisible gas.
questions.explanation: Evaporated water need not be visible to leave a leaf.

questions.prompt: What role do stomata play?
questions.questionText: What role do stomata play?
options: They carry liquid water through the entire stem.
They absorb most soil minerals directly.
They convert all water into sugar.
They are pores that allow gas exchange and water-vapor loss.
questions.correctAnswer: They are pores that allow gas exchange and water-vapor loss.
questions.explanation: Stomata connect internal leaf spaces with the air; their opening affects exchange.

questions.prompt: A plant wilts as water loss exceeds uptake. Which explanation fits?
questions.questionText: A plant wilts as water loss exceeds uptake. Which explanation fits?
options: All stem cells have immediately died.
Cells can lose water pressure that helps keep tissues firm.
The plant has used up every mineral.
The leaves have become a different species.
questions.correctAnswer: Cells can lose water pressure that helps keep tissues firm.
questions.explanation: Loss of cell turgor can cause wilting; wilting alone does not prove permanent death.

questions.prompt: A stem in colored water develops colored lines. What is directly supported?
questions.questionText: A stem in colored water develops colored lines. What is directly supported?
options: The dye became sugar through photosynthesis.
Every cell transported equal amounts of dye.
Colored water moved through some stem tissues.
The stem created the dye itself.
questions.correctAnswer: Colored water moved through some stem tissues.
questions.explanation: Visible dye traces transport but does not establish sugar production or equal flow everywhere.

questions.prompt: A covered-soil plant setup loses 8 g in two hours. What is its average mass-loss rate?
questions.questionText: A covered-soil plant setup loses 8 g in two hours. What is its average mass-loss rate?
options: 8 g per hour.
4 g per hour.
16 g per hour.
2 g per hour.
questions.correctAnswer: 4 g per hour.
questions.explanation: Divide 8 g by 2 hours. The rate is for the measured setup, not automatically pure transpiration.

questions.prompt: Why cover the soil surface in a water-loss study?
questions.questionText: Why cover the soil surface in a water-loss study?
options: To stop all water movement through the plant.
To make leaves photosynthesize without light.
To supply extra minerals from the cover.
To reduce evaporation from soil as an alternative source of mass loss.
questions.correctAnswer: To reduce evaporation from soil as an alternative source of mass loss.
questions.explanation: Covering soil helps distinguish leaf-associated loss from soil evaporation.

questions.prompt: A model shows leaf evaporation -> tension in water columns -> upward water movement. What process does it help explain?
questions.questionText: A model shows leaf evaporation -> tension in water columns -> upward water movement. What process does it help explain?
options: How transpiration contributes to water transport through xylem.
How roots manufacture sunlight.
How leaves pump blood.
How sugar is made from minerals alone.
questions.correctAnswer: How transpiration contributes to water transport through xylem.
questions.explanation: Evaporation can help pull water through connected transport tissues; this is a simplified model.

questions.prompt: Two matched plants have similar stomatal opening, temperature, and water supply. Which air condition tends to favor faster water-vapor loss?
questions.questionText: Two matched plants have similar stomatal opening, temperature, and water supply. Which air condition tends to favor faster water-vapor loss?
options: Drier air.
More humid air.
Air already saturated with water vapor.
Identical humidity in both treatments.
questions.correctAnswer: Drier air.
questions.explanation: A larger difference in water-vapor concentration between leaf and air can favor loss.

questions.prompt: A fan treatment loses 12 g while a matched still-air treatment loses 7 g over the same period. What difference was measured?
questions.questionText: A fan treatment loses 12 g while a matched still-air treatment loses 7 g over the same period. What difference was measured?
options: 19 g more loss with the fan.
7 g less loss with the fan.
5 g more loss with the fan.
Both lost 12 g.
questions.correctAnswer: 5 g more loss with the fan.
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from 12. The experiment must also account for temperature and other conditions.

questions.prompt: Why can moving air increase transpiration under otherwise similar conditions?
questions.questionText: Why can moving air increase transpiration under otherwise similar conditions?
options: It can carry humid air away from the leaf surface.
It creates new water inside roots.
It necessarily opens every stoma fully.
It removes the plant's need for water.
questions.correctAnswer: It can carry humid air away from the leaf surface.
questions.explanation: Moving air can maintain a water-vapor gradient, though plant responses also matter.

questions.prompt: What tradeoff can occur when stomata close during water shortage?
questions.questionText: What tradeoff can occur when stomata close during water shortage?
options: Water loss stops but carbon dioxide enters faster through closed pores.
Roots no longer need water.
All stored sugars instantly disappear.
Water loss can decrease while carbon dioxide entry also decreases.
questions.correctAnswer: Water loss can decrease while carbon dioxide entry also decreases.
questions.explanation: Stomata serve both water balance and gas exchange, linking transpiration to photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Two plants differ in total leaf area. Why compare water loss per unit leaf area?
questions.questionText: Two plants differ in total leaf area. Why compare water loss per unit leaf area?
options: To account for the different amount of leaf surface.
To guarantee their species are identical.
To remove the need to record time.
To prove temperature has no effect.
questions.correctAnswer: To account for the different amount of leaf surface.
questions.explanation: Total loss can differ partly because one plant has more leaf area.

questions.prompt: Plant A loses 10 g from 100 square centimeters of leaves; B loses 15 g from 300 square centimeters over equal times. Which has greater loss per unit area?
questions.questionText: Plant A loses 10 g from 100 square centimeters of leaves; B loses 15 g from 300 square centimeters over equal times. Which has greater loss per unit area?
options: B, because its total loss is larger.
Both, because time was equal.
A, at 0.10 g per square centimeter compared with B's 0.05.
B, at 0.20 g per square centimeter.
questions.correctAnswer: A, at 0.10 g per square centimeter compared with B's 0.05.
questions.explanation: Normalize each total by area before comparing: 10/100 and 15/300.

questions.prompt: A leaf has a waxy surface layer. What function can this structure support?
questions.questionText: A leaf has a waxy surface layer. What function can this structure support?
options: Replacing every root function.
Making water from light.
Reducing water loss through the leaf surface.
Preventing all gas exchange under every condition.
questions.correctAnswer: Reducing water loss through the leaf surface.
questions.explanation: A waxy cuticle helps reduce water loss; stomata still provide regulated exchange.

questions.prompt: A student attributes pot mass loss entirely to transpiration, but water leaked from the base. What is the problem?
questions.questionText: A student attributes pot mass loss entirely to transpiration, but water leaked from the base. What is the problem?
options: Liquid leaving the setup contributes to mass loss too.
Leaks can change only color, not mass.
Transpiration cannot occur in a pot.
A balance cannot measure water loss.
questions.correctAnswer: Liquid leaving the setup contributes to mass loss too.
questions.explanation: Track the system boundary: drainage is another way matter can leave.

questions.prompt: A plant takes up more water than it uses directly in photosynthesis. Is that possible?
questions.questionText: A plant takes up more water than it uses directly in photosynthesis. Is that possible?
options: No; every absorbed molecule must immediately become sugar.
No; roots take up only exactly the water used in sugar production.
Yes; all excess water becomes mineral nutrients.
Yes; much water can be lost through transpiration or retained in tissues.
questions.correctAnswer: Yes; much water can be lost through transpiration or retained in tissues.
questions.explanation: Water has several roles and destinations, so uptake is not a direct measure of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Water is abundant in soil, but damaged roots absorb it slowly. What could happen on a warm day?
questions.questionText: Water is abundant in soil, but damaged roots absorb it slowly. What could happen on a warm day?
options: Leaves must stay firm because the soil is wet.
Root damage necessarily increases uptake.
The plant no longer exchanges gases.
Leaves may lose water faster than roots replace it.
questions.correctAnswer: Leaves may lose water faster than roots replace it.
questions.explanation: Soil availability and the plant's ability to take up water are separate factors.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly tests the root-to-leaf transport model?
questions.questionText: Which observation most directly tests the root-to-leaf transport model?
options: A water tracer appears in stem conducting tissues and then in leaves.
A leaf's outline resembles another leaf.
The pot changes position in a room.
The plant is taller than its label.
questions.correctAnswer: A water tracer appears in stem conducting tissues and then in leaves.
questions.explanation: Tracer location over time can provide evidence about a transport pathway.

questions.prompt: A humid-air treatment and dry-air treatment also use different temperatures. Can the result isolate humidity?
questions.questionText: A humid-air treatment and dry-air treatment also use different temperatures. Can the result isolate humidity?
options: Yes; temperature never affects water movement.
Yes; two treatments always isolate one factor.
No; temperature is another changed variable.
No; humidity cannot be investigated.
questions.correctAnswer: No; temperature is another changed variable.
questions.explanation: To isolate humidity, keep other relevant conditions comparable or measure their effects.

questions.prompt: A setup loses 9 g in three hours; a comparison loses 6 g in two hours. Which rate comparison is correct?
questions.questionText: A setup loses 9 g in three hours; a comparison loses 6 g in two hours. Which rate comparison is correct?
options: The first is faster because 9 is larger.
The second averages 6 g per hour.
Both average 3 g per hour.
The first averages 27 g per hour.
questions.correctAnswer: Both average 3 g per hour.
questions.explanation: Loss divided by duration is 3 g per hour for both.

questions.prompt: After drought, stomatal closure reduces loss even though air is very dry. What should a model include?
questions.questionText: After drought, stomatal closure reduces loss even though air is very dry. What should a model include?
options: Only humidity, because stomata never respond.
Both the air conditions and the plant's regulation of pores.
Only leaf color.
A rule that drier air always produces unlimited loss.
questions.correctAnswer: Both the air conditions and the plant's regulation of pores.
questions.explanation: Environmental effects and biological regulation interact; one factor alone may not predict the result.

questions.prompt: A sealed bag around leaves develops condensation. Why include a similarly placed empty bag?
questions.questionText: A sealed bag around leaves develops condensation. Why include a similarly placed empty bag?
options: To prove the leaves contain no water.
To measure root length from bag color.
To stop the plant's respiration.
To check for moisture already present or condensing without leaves.
questions.correctAnswer: To check for moisture already present or condensing without leaves.
questions.explanation: A comparison helps assess alternative moisture sources; condensation alone needs careful interpretation.

questions.prompt: A celery stalk's dyed region expands over time. Can this determine the exact transpiration rate?
questions.questionText: A celery stalk's dyed region expands over time. Can this determine the exact transpiration rate?
options: Yes; every centimeter equals one gram for all stalks.
Not by itself; transport distance is not a direct measure of water volume lost per time.
Yes; dye concentration cannot affect visibility.
No; colored water can never move in xylem.
questions.correctAnswer: Not by itself; transport distance is not a direct measure of water volume lost per time.
questions.explanation: Visible progress demonstrates movement but is not a calibrated loss-rate measurement.

questions.prompt: A model sends all absorbed soil minerals into the air with evaporating water. What revision is needed?
questions.questionText: A model sends all absorbed soil minerals into the air with evaporating water. What revision is needed?
options: Keep the model because minerals evaporate just like water.
Show water vapor leaving while dissolved minerals generally remain in the plant.
Show minerals turning into water vapor.
Remove root uptake because minerals cannot move.
questions.correctAnswer: Show water vapor leaving while dissolved minerals generally remain in the plant.
questions.explanation: Evaporation separates water from dissolved materials; minerals do not normally leave as water vapor.

questions.prompt: A shade treatment loses less mass than a sun treatment. What limits the conclusion that light alone caused the difference?
questions.questionText: A shade treatment loses less mass than a sun treatment. What limits the conclusion that light alone caused the difference?
options: Sunlight may also change leaf temperature and stomatal behavior.
Both samples contain leaves.
Both masses were measured in grams.
The measurements used the same time interval.
questions.correctAnswer: Sunlight may also change leaf temperature and stomatal behavior.
questions.explanation: Several linked factors can change with sunlight, so the mechanism needs more evidence.

questions.prompt: A covered-soil plant setup loses 14 g; an otherwise comparable covered-soil setup without a plant loses 2 g. What is the difference?
questions.questionText: A covered-soil plant setup loses 14 g; an otherwise comparable covered-soil setup without a plant loses 2 g. What is the difference?
options: 16 g, all caused by the plant.
12 g, associated with the plant under these conditions.
2 g, because only the comparison counts.
14 g, with no need to consider background loss.
questions.correctAnswer: 12 g, associated with the plant under these conditions.
questions.explanation: Subtract background loss: 14 - 2 = 12. A comparison improves interpretation but is still a model of the sources.

questions.prompt: A plant wilts at noon and becomes firm later without new watering. Which explanation is plausible?
questions.questionText: A plant wilts at noon and becomes firm later without new watering. Which explanation is plausible?
options: Wilting always means the plant died and returned to life.
Lower water loss later allowed uptake to restore tissue water balance.
All water was created from darkness.
The plant stopped containing cells.
questions.correctAnswer: Lower water loss later allowed uptake to restore tissue water balance.
questions.explanation: Changing loss and uptake rates can allow recovery of cell water pressure.

questions.prompt: A report uses daily pot mass loss to claim a plant's exact photosynthesis rate. What is the best criticism?
questions.questionText: A report uses daily pot mass loss to claim a plant's exact photosynthesis rate. What is the best criticism?
options: Mass can never be useful in plant studies.
Photosynthesis and transpiration are the same process.
Every gram lost necessarily equals one gram of sugar made.
Water loss includes transpiration and possibly other pathways, not just water used in sugar production.
questions.correctAnswer: Water loss includes transpiration and possibly other pathways, not just water used in sugar production.
questions.explanation: Related plant processes require different measurements; one cannot substitute directly for another.
